opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so with Toolformer, the core idea was to teach a model to use tools in a self-supervised way. The model would sample places in text where calling an API — a calculator, a search engine, a calendar, a translation system — might help, actually execute those calls, and then keep only the ones that reduced the perplexity on the following tokens. That worked surprisingly well, but it had real limitations.

The biggest one was that it was fundamentally a single-step, one-tool-at-a-time setup, and it was baked in at the data level. Each tool needed its own pipeline of sampling and filtering, and the model learned to call that specific set of tools. If you wanted to add a new tool, you basically had to regenerate data and fine-tune again. It didn't really compose tools, it didn't chain calls, it didn't do interactive back-and-forth with the result.

What we realized is that the much more scalable path is a model that can just read a description of a tool, or a few examples, in context, and then follow that — the way a human reads documentation. And that's really an instruction-following capability. If the model is good at following instructions, then "here's an API, here's what it does, here's how to call it" becomes just another instruction. You get zero-shot tool use for free, essentially, and you can plug in tools you never trained on.

So in a sense, extending Toolformer wasn't about building a fancier Toolformer. It was about making the base model aligned and good at following instructions, because that's what unlocks general tool use. That's a big part of why, after Toolformer, a lot of the focus shifted to instruction tuning and RLHF in Llama 2 — and then you saw tool use emerge much more naturally on top of that, even capabilities we hadn't explicitly trained for, like the model figuring out how to use tools in a temporally coherent way. Instruction following was the foundation; tools were one of the things it made possible.

r001.rationale: The response says that strong instruction-following is what unlocks general tool use and was the foundation for extending beyond Toolformer’s limitations.

r002.rationale: It credits instruction-following and instruction tuning for enabling tool use, but does not attribute agents’ practical effectiveness to crossing a threshold of underlying model intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
So Toolformer was really a proof of concept. The core idea was self-supervised: you take a language model, you let it annotate its own pretraining data with API calls, you filter those calls by whether they actually reduce perplexity on the following tokens, and then you fine-tune on that. It worked, and it was elegant because you didn't need humans in the loop labeling tool calls. But it had real limitations.

The first limitation was that the model learned to call tools in a very narrow, almost reflexive way. It would insert a calculator call or a Wikipedia search in the middle of a sentence because that pattern helped predict the next few tokens. That's not the same as reasoning about when a tool is useful. And crucially, it couldn't chain tools. It couldn't say, "I'll search for this, then take the result and compute something with it, then decide if I need another search." Each call was essentially independent.

And when we asked ourselves why, the answer was pretty clear: the base models we were working with at the time, GPT-J and similar, just couldn't follow instructions. You couldn't tell them, "here are the tools available, here is how to use them, now solve this problem step by step." They didn't have that capability. So you were stuck with this bootstrapping trick where the model had to discover tool usage implicitly from the data.

Once you have a model that actually follows instructions, the whole problem changes. You can describe the tool in natural language. You can show a few examples in context. You can have the model plan, call a tool, observe the result, and decide what to do next. That's where things like interactive, multi-step tool use become possible, which is what we were pushing toward. So in a sense, better instruction-following wasn't an improvement on top of Toolformer, it was a prerequisite to go beyond what Toolformer could do. That's part of why I shifted my focus to the Llama 2 and Llama 3 post-training work. You need the foundation of a model that understands what you're asking before you can teach it to use tools in a general way.

r001.rationale: The response says better instruction-following was a prerequisite for moving beyond Toolformer’s implicit, independent tool calls to interactive, multi-step tool use.

r002.rationale: It links effective multi-step tool use to a capable underlying model: earlier models could not follow instructions, while a model that could follow them could plan, use tools, and respond to results.

astra-6.text:
The idea with Toolformer was to teach a model to use tools—to call an API and use the result. But that’s only one part of building an assistant. You also need the model to understand what you’re asking, choose the right tool for that request, and keep working toward your goal.

If the underlying model doesn’t follow instructions reliably, it’s difficult to build that broader behavior on top. So better instruction following was a foundation for extending Toolformer from learning individual tool calls toward an assistant that could actually carry out a user’s task.

r001.rationale: It says reliable instruction following is a foundation for extending Toolformer beyond individual tool calls.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliable instruction following, but does not attribute agents’ practical effectiveness to crossing a threshold of underlying model intelligence.

sol-6.1.text: With Toolformer, we showed that a language model could learn to call tools, but that’s only one part of what you want from an assistant. You want to give it an instruction, have it understand the task, and then use the appropriate tools to complete it. Those are different capabilities. A model can learn when to call a calculator without being very good at following your request. So, to go further—to have more complex interactions, potentially with several tool calls—we needed a stronger instruction-following model as the foundation.

r001.rationale: It says extending Toolformer to handle more complex interactions required a stronger instruction-following model as the foundation.

r002.rationale: It describes stronger instruction-following as necessary, but does not attribute agents’ practical effectiveness to crossing a threshold of underlying model intelligence.
